title: Reading PostgreSQL plans
summary: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) node by node: estimated against actual rows, loops, time and buffers, and the two fixes they usually point to.

steps.title: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
body: Production runs PostgreSQL, and its plans carry more than SQLite's: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` **runs** the query and prints, for every node, what the planner expected and what really happened.
- A plan is a tree. Each node pulls rows from the nodes indented under it; read it from the innermost node outwards.
- `(cost=0.00..69351.00 rows=58 width=24)` is the **estimate**: cost in planner units (not milliseconds), rows it expected, bytes per row.
- `(actual time=0.412..402.201 rows=61 loops=1)` is **what happened**: milliseconds to the first and last row, rows produced, and how many times the node ran. Time and rows are **per loop**.

- `Buffers: shared hit=2117 read=29734`: 8 kB pages found in PostgreSQL's cache (hit) or fetched from the OS or disk (read). Since PostgreSQL 18, `ANALYZE` includes buffers by default, prints actual rows with decimals (`rows=61.00`) and adds `Index Searches` to index scans.
- `Rows Removed by Filter` is work thrown away.
Below: the customer order history, before and after an index on `orders (customer_id, placed_at DESC)`. Note `ANALYZE` executes the statement: wrap an UPDATE or DELETE in `BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;`.

pgplan.query:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, placed_at, total_cents FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY placed_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
text: Limit  (cost=69352.31..69352.36 rows=20 width=24) (actual time=402.315..402.322 rows=20 loops=1)
->  Sort  (cost=69352.31..69352.46 rows=58 width=24) (actual time=402.313..402.317 rows=20 loops=1)
->  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..69351.00 rows=58 width=24) (actual time=0.412..402.201 rows=61 loops=1)
after: Limit  (cost=0.43..80.12 rows=20 width=24) (actual time=0.031..0.068 rows=20 loops=1)
->  Index Scan using ix_orders_customer_placed on orders  (cost=0.43..231.53 rows=58 width=24) (actual time=0.030..0.064 rows=20 loops=1)
pgplan.note: After: the estimate says 58 rows but the index scan produced 20. That is not a bad estimate: the Limit above it stopped asking after 20. Compare estimates and actuals on nodes that ran to completion.

steps.prompt: In the *before* plan, where did the 402 ms go?
options: Reading all 3 million orders (about 32,000 pages, most of them from disk) to keep 61
steps.explain: The Seq Scan finishes at 402.2 ms of the 402.4 total; the Sort above it adds almost nothing (a top-N heapsort of 61 rows). `Rows Removed by Filter: 2999939` and `read=29734` say why.

steps.title: Estimated against actual: when the planner guesses wrong
body: The planner picks a plan from its **estimates**, which come from table statistics. When the statistics are stale, it plans for a world that does not exist.

Last night an import added 48,000 orders with `status = 'imported'`. The statistics still say almost no rows have that status, so the planner expects **1** row and chooses a nested loop: for each order, look up its customer by primary key. Fine for 1 row; for 48,210 it does 48,210 index lookups (`loops=48210`).

Read the inner node carefully: `actual time=0.194..0.195 rows=1 loops=48210` means 0.195 ms **each time**, times 48,210 loops: about 9.4 seconds. Per-loop numbers are the most common misreading of a plan.
After `ANALYZE orders;` the estimate is 48,190, and the planner switches to a hash join: read the customers once, build a hash table, stream the orders through it.

pgplan.query:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.id, c.email
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'imported';
text: Nested Loop  (cost=0.85..16.90 rows=1 width=40) (actual time=0.052..9531.774 rows=48210 loops=1)
->  Index Scan using ix_orders_status on orders o  (cost=0.43..8.45 rows=1 width=16) (actual time=0.031..112.406 rows=48210 loops=1)
->  Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers c  (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1 width=32) (actual time=0.194..0.195 rows=1 loops=48210)
after: Hash Join  (cost=2958.00..8197.17 rows=48190 width=40) (actual time=24.310..71.904 rows=48210 loops=1)
->  Bitmap Heap Scan on orders o  (cost=915.91..5114.53 rows=48190 width=16) (actual time=6.102..32.733 rows=48210 loops=1)
->  Bitmap Index Scan on ix_orders_status  (cost=0.00..903.86 rows=48190 width=0) (actual time=4.981..4.981 rows=48210 loops=1)
->  Seq Scan on customers c  (cost=0.00..1708.00 rows=100000 width=32) (actual time=0.010..6.120 rows=100000 loops=1)

steps.prompt: A plan node reads `(cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1 width=32) (actual time=0.194..0.195 rows=1 loops=48210)`. How long did this node take in total?
options: It cannot be known from the plan
steps.explain: Actual time is per loop: 0.195 ms times 48,210 loops is about 9,400 ms. The cost numbers are planner units, never milliseconds.

steps.prompt: Match each PostgreSQL plan node to what it does.
pairs: reads every page of the table
walks the index, fetching each matching row from the table
`Index Only Scan using ix on orders`
answers from the index alone (if the visibility map allows)
`Bitmap Heap Scan` over a `Bitmap Index Scan`
collects matching row locations first, then reads the pages in order
builds a hash table from one input and probes it with the other
for every row of the outer input, runs the inner node again

steps.prompt: Healthy, or worth a closer look?
items: `rows=1` estimated, `rows=480000` actual on a join input
`Rows Removed by Filter: 4999988` on a query that returns 12 rows
steps.explain: Small tables are cheapest to scan. Big estimate gaps mean stale statistics or correlated columns; an external merge sort spilled to disk (raise `work_mem` for that query, or give it an index in the right order); huge filtered-out counts mean a missing index.

steps.prompt: A report got slow after a big import. Put the investigation in order.
lines: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the report query
Find the node where estimated and actual rows differ most
Run ANALYZE on the tables that node reads
Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) again and compare the plan
If the estimate is still far off, look at the WHERE columns (correlated columns, extended statistics)

steps.title: The same fix, proven in SQLite
prompt: The *before* plan above came from the customer order history. Reproduce the fix on the SQLite copy of the table:
2. Return customer **42**'s **20 newest** orders: **id**, **placed_at**, **total_cents**, newest first.
Use the **▤ Query plan** button: with the index, SQLite searches it and needs no temp B-tree for the sort.
solution: CREATE INDEX ix_orders_customer_placed ON orders (customer_id, placed_at);
setup: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL, placed_at TEXT NOT NULL, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL);

WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 30000) INSERT INTO orders SELECT i, (i * 7919) % 500 + 1, datetime('2026-01-01', '+' || (i * 15) || ' minutes'), (i * 37) % 9000 + 500 FROM n;
hints: Equality column first, then the sort column: `(customer_id, placed_at)`.
An ascending index serves `ORDER BY placed_at DESC` too: the database walks it backwards.
steps.explain: Same answer, and the plan changes from a scan plus sort to one index search. In PostgreSQL you would build it with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on the live table.
